section_1.title: What is a Vector? (Visualizing Magnitude & Direction)
section_1.content: Define a vector as a directed line segment. Introduce the concept of a coordinate system where a vector is an arrow starting from the origin (0,0) to a point (x,y).
section_1.example: A GPS coordinate tracking a bird flying from its nest at (0,0) to a tree at (3,2).

section_2.title: Vector Addition: The Parallelogram Rule
section_2.content: Explain how to add two vectors visually. Place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first. The result is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.
section_2.example: A boat moving across a river: Vector A is the boat's speed, Vector B is the river's current. The resulting movement is Vector A + Vector B.

section_3.title: Scalar Multiplication: Stretching the Arrow
section_3.content: Introduce multiplying a vector by a scalar (a real number). Explain that it changes the vector's length (scaling) and can reverse its direction if the scalar is negative.
section_3.example: A superhero 'scaling' their jump: If Vector V is a 2-meter jump, 3V is a 6-meter leap, and -1V is jumping backwards.

section_4.title: Linear Combinations and Basis Vectors
section_4.content: Explain how any 2D vector can be formed by combining the unit vectors 'i' (1,0) and 'j' (0,1). This introduces the concept of the 'span' of a vector space.
section_4.example: A 2D game character moving on a grid: Any movement can be broken down into 'x' horizontal steps and 'y' vertical steps.

section_5.title: Conclusion: The Power of Linear Transformations
section_5.content: Briefly summarize how these basic operations allow us to move, rotate, and resize entire spaces, forming the foundation of computer graphics and AI.
section_5.example: The 'pinch-to-zoom' gesture on a smartphone screen, which is mathematically just a matrix transformation applied to a grid of vectors.
